1. The animation compares two kinds of income check. A "level check" stays the same dollar amount every year. A "rising check" goes up with prices. The frames use US consumer prices (CPI-U) from Aug 2006 to Aug 2026 as the backdrop. They're labeled "illustrative" and "history, not a forecast."

2. A line traces the price history, then a second line for the level check slides steadily downward. Markers then appear at year 5 and at year 20. At year 5 the caption says the level check is worth "about 9 in 10." At year 20 the caption says the rising check is "there," meaning it is back at the first check's level. A "?" appears in the last two frames.

3. A fixed payment buys less each year as prices rise. The level check is worth about 90% of its original buying power by year 5, and the gap keeps widening to year 20. A check that rises with inflation keeps roughly the buying power of the first check.

   I'm reading the "there after 20 years" caption and the faint yellow line as meaning the rising check holds its value. They're a little ambiguous, so I'm not certain of that reading.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that inflation matters when comparing a fixed payout with one that rises. The image shows nothing about how much less the rising option pays at the start, so it can't tell anyone which to pick.

5. The animation didn't suggest that advice. The "?" only poses an open question, and the takeaway in 4 is my own conclusion.
